# Surucijātaka (Ja 489)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Surucijātaka* (Ja 489, PTS Ja IV 314ff.) is a canonical birth story in the Pali Jātaka collection [Fausböll 1887; Collins 2016]. According to its opening frame, the Buddha related the narrative while residing near Sāvatthī at the mansion of Migāra's mother (*Migāramātupāsāda*), occasioned by the eight boons granted to the lay disciple Visākhā [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1887]. Set in Mithilā during the reign of King Suruci, the story of the past follows Prince Suruci (*Surucikumāro*), who travels to Takkasilā to acquire arts [Fausböll 1887]. In the narrative, a childless royal couple prays for a son; Sakka is stirred by Queen Sumedhā's prayer, questions her concerning her virtues, and grants her boon [Anandajoti 2010]. When a palace is planned for the royal prince, the king summons master geomancers (*vatthuvijjācariya*) to locate an auspicious construction site [Mus 1935]. In the story's resolution (*samodhāna*), Prince Mahāpanāda is identified with Bhaddaji, Queen Sumedhā with Visākhā, Vissakamma with Ānanda, and Sakka with the Buddha himself [Fausböll 1887].
The text has drawn attention from modern scholars for its treatment of domestic life, marital fidelity, and gender relations [Collins 2016; Cabezón 2017]. It is frequently cited as one of the few Buddhist narrative texts extolling monogamy, while also vividly portraying the misery and jealousy of co-wives (*sapattiyo*) as a distinctive hardship experienced by women in polygynous royal households [Collins 2016; Cabezón 2017]. The tale also extols the domestic ethics of a virtuous wife who behaves compassionately toward her husband, in-laws, co-wives, servants, and mendicants, promising earthly and celestial rewards for such virtues [Lewis & Tuladhar 2000].
SuttaCentral notes verse and passage parallels with the *Mittātherīgāthā* (Thig 2.7), *Nimijātaka* (Ja 541), *Catumahārājasutta* (AN 3.37), *Dutiyacatumahārājasutta* (AN 3.38), and *Sānusutta* (SN 10.5), as well as thematic allusions across several *Vimānavatthu* stories (Vv 15, 19, 22–25, 37, 52) and the *Petavatthu* (Pv 39) [SuttaCentral]. DharmaNexus confirms substantial text reuse with the *Nimijātaka* (Ja 541 §14.1–14.6), the *Tikanipāta* (AN 3), the *Yakkha Saṁyutta* (SN 10), and the commentaries to the Jātaka, Vimānavatthu, and Dhammapada [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also aligns segments of the story with Kṣemendra's Tibetan *Bodhisatvāvadānakalpalatā* (D4155) [DharmaNexus].
